description: Team AETHELGARD is from Peshawar, Pakistan. Yasher Ahmad, our team lead, is a self-taught robotics engineer who also builds our 3D models and animations, and Yahya Bashir builds with him. We like taking hard engineering and turning it into something people can play with. For Space Apps 2026 we made Downlink, a 3D browser game where you design a CubeSat, defend it in a design review and fly it. We would love teammates who are good at storytelling, sound design, physics or teaching.
summary:
In school, space missions are taught as formulas on a page, so students never feel why engineers keep spare power, extra checks and backups on a satellite. Downlink is a free 3D browser game that makes them feel it. Players build a small CubeSat from real parts, get it through a design review where 8 of 10 checks must pass, launch it, and fly a one-year mission in which problems happen in orbit. The spare they kept (their margins) is what saves the satellite, and the mission report explains which choice helped and which hurt.

The rules come from NASA resources: JPL Concept Maturity Levels set the margins and the review, CubeSat 101 sets the size, weight, launch and first-hour timeline, and NASA Planetary Fact Sheets drive the orbit and solar power physics. Every number in the game shows which document it came from. It runs from a link on any laptop, with no install and no login, and up to four students can play together on one screen, each with a role. It matters because it gives students without a space lab, such as schools in Pakistan, a hands-on feel for how real missions are designed.
details:
What it does. Downlink is a 3D space mission design game that runs in the browser. The player picks a science objective (watch hurricanes form, monitor crops and wildfires, or measure space weather), a study level, a cost cap and a schedule. In the Design Lab they fit solar panels, a battery, a flight computer, attitude control, an instrument and antennas onto a 3U CubeSat shown in 3D in a cleanroom, and choose a ground station and orbit. A dashboard recalculates ten checks after every change: dry mass, power, battery energy, flight software and link margins, budget reserve, launcher compatibility, instrument fit, data downlinked, and schedule and risk.

The design matures through JPL Concept Maturity Levels 1 to 4, shown as a meter: fit the right instrument, save and compare two designs, then bring every margin up to the NASA threshold. A design review passes the design when 8 of 10 checks are met. The flight shows the lift-off as a shared-ride payload, release from the deployer, antenna deployment at 30 minutes and first beacon at 45 minutes (CubeSat 101), then a time-lapse of a year of science operations. Seeded events (a stuck antenna, a radiation upset, a ground-station outage, an ageing battery) are absorbed if the player built in the matching margin or backup, and otherwise force a decision that costs something. The mission report scores five categories and explains each score in one sentence with a suggested fix, then the player can revise and refly.

How it works. A small simulation written for the game computes orbit period and eclipse time from Earth's gravitational parameter and radius, solar power from panel area and solar irradiance, battery load through eclipse, a link budget for each antenna against the chosen ground station, data returned per day, cost and build time. 33 automated tests check it. Every value in the game's data tables carries a source: a NASA document, or "Game balance" where we chose a value for play, and the game shows that tag next to the number.

Benefits. It teaches that mission design is trading limited mass, power, data, money and time against a science goal, and it shows why margins exist by letting the player meet the failure each one protects against. A weak design is never just "red": the report says which choice caused which loss. It is free, open source, needs only a browser and a link, and one laptop serves a group: two to four players share the screen as Mission Lead, Spacecraft Engineer, Science Officer, and Comms and Ops, each with a priority card that pulls against the others, so the team has to negotiate like a real mission team.

Our goals. Give students and teachers without a space lab a hands-on first experience of mission design. Next we want to add a Moon mission, an Urdu version, and test it in Peshawar schools.

Tools, languages and software. JavaScript (ES modules), HTML and CSS; three.js for 3D rendering; Vite as the build tool; Blender 5.2 for the 3D models and animations, made by the team; Web Audio API for sound (synthesised in code, no audio files); Vercel for hosting; GitHub for source. No hardware beyond a laptop.

Limits. One spacecraft class today (CubeSats in low Earth orbit). The simulation is simplified for learning; values not taken from NASA sources are labelled "Game balance".

Play: https://downlink-eight.vercel.app/
